A striking feature in Wutun phonology is the absence of tones, which separates Wutun from most of the Sinitic languages. Due to language contact with neighboring non-Sinitic languages (notably Amdo Tibetan and Bonan), Wutun seems to have lost tones that it originally had on the some earlier stage of its development. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-contrastive and falls regularly on the final syllable of bi- and polysyllabic words; the language has lost tone and has no phonologically distinctive suprasegmentals at word level (stress is predictable, not phonemic).
new_statements.exceptions: None given; author notes (p. 3) that Wutun 'has not developed any phonologically relevant suprasegmental distinctions (such as stress system)' — i.e. final stress is phonetic/predictable, not contrastive. Long/tense /ii/, /uu/ may be traces of an earlier tonal opposition (p. 41). Phonology chapter based on one male speaker (Xiawu Dongzhou, b. 1966) with noted inter-speaker variation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, illustrated with isolated citation forms of 2-4 syllables (including reduplicated and polysyllabic native words); no discussion of stress in affixed/cliticized words or phrase-level prosody.
new_statements.identity_note: Sandman 2016 describes Wutun proper (Wutun/Sangeshong villages, Tongren/Rebgong County, Huangnan Prefecture, Qinghai; ISO wuh), phonology based on one speaker from Wutun (Xiawu Dongzhou, b. 1966). Glottolog 5.1 also files Zhou Chenlei's works on Zhoutun (周屯话, Guide County, Qinghai; Zhou 2016 Nankai diss., Zhou 2022 Routledge 'Zhoutun') under wutu1241, but Zhoutun is a different Sinitic contact variety in a different county and should not be conflated with Wutun; those works were not used here.

sources.note: Section 2.4 'Word stress' (pp. 40-41): word stress in bi- and polysyllabic words falls regularly on the final syllable (lhakang [ɬa.'kʰɑ̃], galamala [ka.la.ma.'la]); Wutun has lost tones; 'best described as a language with no phonologically relevant suprasegmental distinctions at the level of isolated words'. Also p. 3: Wutun has not developed any phonologically relevant suprasegmental distinctions (such as stress system) to compensate the loss of tones.
